exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criteria 2 (3D/volumetric) and 3 (organ segmentation). (1) The SW-DNN (DeepLabv3+/ResNet101 variant) processes 2D CT slices independently: the input is explicitly defined as x ∈ R^(w×h), data augmentation is applied per-slice ('the CT slice was randomly flipped horizontally'), and there are no 3D convolutions or volumetric context. Although the authors report '3D-based evaluations' of DSC/TPVF/PPV, this only means volumetric metrics were computed after stacking 2D slice predictions — the model itself has no 3D context (exclusion criterion 3). (2) The segmentation target is the clinical target volume (CTV) for stomach cancer radiotherapy, described as 'tissues of potential tumors or subclinical diseases that are barely detectable in CT images' — a radiotherapy target/tumor-related volume, not an anatomical organ (exclusion criterion 5).
screening_notes: All other criteria are satisfied: deep learning is the primary method (SW-DNN, a novel stochastic-width modification of DeepLabv3+); CT modality is used (150 planning CT scans from West China Hospital); quantitative metrics are reported (DSC 0.7457 2D / 0.7530 3D, TPVF, PPV, with t-tests); and there is a clear methodological contribution (SW mechanism on shortcut connections). However, the two disqualifying criteria are unambiguous: the network is strictly 2D slice-based despite volumetric metric evaluation, and CTV delineation is target-volume (tumor-inclusive) segmentation rather than organ segmentation, which is out of scope for a review on 3D organ segmentation. No extraction performed per protocol.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (Exclusion Criterion 3; fails Inclusion Criterion 2)
screening_notes: The paper meets most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (SANet with HRNet-w18 encoder, novel Scale Attention Module), organs (colon, small intestine, duodenum) are segmented from CT with quantitative metrics (DSC, HD95, RVD, CD). However, the model is strictly 2D: 'All the 3D CT scans were converted into 2D slices for model training' and 'all CT scans were inferred in a slice-by-slice manner. Then the slices from the same scan were stacked into a 3D volume for evaluation.' No 3D convolutions or interslice context are used; stacking is performed only post-hoc for volumetric metric computation. The authors themselves list as a limitation that 'the proposed 2D input for SANet might cause some loss of spatial information and consistency along z-direction compared with 3D input.' This is 2D-slice-independent processing, explicitly excluded by criterion 3. Slight residual ambiguity because evaluation is volumetric and 3D visualizations are provided, hence confidence 0.85 rather than higher.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (Exclusion criterion 3). The paper explicitly uses a 2D VGG16 U-Net applied to independently processed 2D slices (resampled to 128×128 pixels; 16,151 2D training images), and the authors state: 'The main limitation of this study lies in the implementation of a 2D architecture, when several 3D networks have been already effectively proposed for this purpose.' While Dice is computed over whole 3D volumes for evaluation, the network architecture and inference operate purely per-slice with no 3D context, failing Inclusion criterion 2.
screening_notes: Paper meets several criteria: deep learning (U-Net CNN) is the primary method, CT modality (contrast-enhanced renal CT), kidney segmentation (organ-level, plus tumor/cyst), and extensive quantitative evaluation (Dice, ASD, RCC, RIU, UA). However, it fails the 3D/volumetric requirement: the model is an explicitly acknowledged 2D architecture with no 3D convolution or volumetric context. Additionally, the contribution is primarily a comparative evaluation of existing uncertainty quantification techniques (MC Dropout, DropConnect, ensembles, TTA) on a standard benchmark U-Net rather than a novel segmentation architecture (weakening Inclusion criterion 6 / triggering Exclusion criterion 7), though this is secondary to the decisive 2D-processing exclusion. Not a framework paper (no open-source toolkit presented), so framework routing/template not applicable.

exclusion_reason: Fails criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric): the iCurveE model is explicitly described by the authors as having a '2D architecture' (U-Net backbone with Res-SE blocks), i.e., 2D slice-based processing with no 3D context reported — matching exclusion criterion 3 ('Only processes 2D slices without 3D context'). Additionally, the paper's contribution is prospective clinical validation of a pre-existing, proprietary commercial auto-segmentation tool (iCurveE, NMPA Class III approved, developed by PVmed on a separate retrospective dataset), not a novel segmentation method or architecture (include criterion 6 not met; exclude criterion 7 arguably applies).
screening_notes: The paper meets criteria 1 (DL is primary method: U-Net backbone with Res-SE blocks), 3 (segments 11 thoracic OARs: lungs, trachea, bronchial tree, aorta, heart, esophagus, liver, humeral heads, spinal cord), 4 (planning CT scans from 500 patients), and 5 (quantitative metrics: vDSC 0.896 for AI, HD95 5.62 mm, sDSC, contouring time). However, it fails criterion 2: the Discussion explicitly states 'the model's 2D architecture', and no 3D convolutions or 3D contextual processing are described; evaluation is volumetric but the method itself is 2D slice-based. Furthermore, the architectural description is minimal (details deferred to supplementary tables), the code is proprietary and not available, and the core novelty is trial design/clinical evidence (physician-AI interaction, variability reduction, dosimetric impact) rather than a methodological contribution to 3D organ segmentation. Borderline aspects noted: it benchmarks against 3D methods (nnU-Net vDSC 0.850, TotalSegmentator vDSC 0.781), which a lenient reading could justify inclusion; hence confidence is 0.8 rather than higher.

exclusion_reason: Fails 3D requirement: CNN is trained and evaluated on individual 2D CT slices (361 slices from 10 patients, augmented to 24,052 slices); the 3D polygon model is assembled afterward without 3D volumetric context or 3D convolutions. Additionally, it is a one-page conference abstract applying existing CNN techniques for surgical workflow acceleration with no methodological contribution (criterion 7) and minimal evaluation (single IoU of 0.85, no Dice/Hausdorff, no comparison methods).
screening_notes: Deep learning (CNN) is the primary method and CT is the modality, and the heart is the target structure, but processing is 2D slice-based only; 3D model creation is post-hoc polygon reconstruction, not 3D segmentation. Tiny training set (10 patients), no comparison to other methods, no per-structure metrics. Would not meet inclusion criteria 2 (3D/volumetric) and arguably 6 (novel contribution).

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (Exclusion criterion 7)
screening_notes: Criteria 1-5 are met: DL is the primary method, 3D CT volumes processed (hybrid 2D+3D branch), liver is segmented (plus tumor) from CT (LiTS + private scans), Dice global 96.2% reported. However, the method section describes a re-implementation of H-DenseUNet (Li et al. 2017, ref [46]) with Han's ResNet-based liver localization (ref [45]): the pipeline (ResNet ROI, 2D Dense-UNet + 3D Dense-UNet, feature fusion layer) is cited directly to these prior works rather than presented as modified. The only additions are standard histogram equalization preprocessing and morphological postprocessing — no new architecture, loss, training scheme, ablation, or comparison table is presented, and the single 96.2% global Dice on a mixed 35-scan test set is not shown to improve on the original H-DenseUNet results. The genuine contribution is the surgical-applicability discussion, which is not a methodological contribution under the inclusion criteria. Borderline call: a lenient reading of 'hybrid network' as the authors' contribution would flip this to INCLUDE.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context: the proposed MPN is a 2D U-Net variant trained and applied slice-wise; the sole 3D model (V-Net) is an existing baseline used for comparison, not the paper's contribution
screening_notes: Passes DL-primary (DCNN/U-Net variant), CT modality, organ segmentation (lungs), quantitative evaluation (Dice 0.9845, IoU 0.9697, HD 3.7480, nodule coverage 87.54%), and novelty (multi-scale prediction heads + residual blocks). Fails criterion 2 (3D/volumetric): paper states 'All experiments used 2-D slice-wise training set except the experiment for V-Net' and reports Hausdorff as 'average 2-D slice-wise'; MPN uses no 3D convolutions or volumetric context. This triggers exclusion rule 3 and fails include-criterion 2. Residual uncertainty (0.2): scan-level evaluation and comparison against a 3D baseline could be argued as partial 3D relevance by a lenient reviewer.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (exclusion criterion 3; fails inclusion criterion 2: 3D/volumetric processing)
screening_notes: The paper proposes DD-UNet++ (standard U-Net++ with standard convolutions replaced by dilated convolutions in the two deepest layers, dilation rates 1/2/4/8) for segmenting bladder, rectum, and CTV on pelvic CT images of 70 post-hysterectomy patients (~13,000 slices, ~11,000 annotated). It satisfies most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (criterion 1 ✓), CT modality (criterion 4 ✓), organ segmentation including OARs (bladder, rectum) plus CTV (criterion 3 ✓), quantitative Dice evaluation (criterion 5 ✓), and a modest novel architectural modification (criterion 6 ✓). However, the network operates strictly on individual 2D slices: 'During the testing phase, all 2D CT sections in the test set were tested one by one. The input is a two-dimensional CT image, and the final output is a pixel-level classification.' There are no 3D convolutions, no adjacent-slice stacking, and no volumetric context modeling — the dilated convolutions enlarge only the in-plane (2D) receptive field. This matches exclusion criterion 3 ('Only processes 2D slices without 3D context') and fails the mandatory inclusion criterion 2 (processes 3D CT volumes, not just 2D slices independently).

exclusion_reason: Deep learning is not the primary segmentation method — segmentation uses classical methods only (Graph-Cut, improved Hessian filter, adaptive multi-scale region growing); no CNN/U-Net/Transformer anywhere. Additionally, no quantitative segmentation metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff) are reported — evaluation is limited to rendering FPS and a single-case tumor volume comparison (533ml predicted vs 512ml resected).
screening_notes: SPIE Medical Imaging 2016 system/platform paper describing RayPlus, a web-based (B/S) liver surgery planning tool. Processes 3D CT volumes and segments liver/vessels/tumor, but via interactive Graph-Cut and filter+region-growing pipelines, not deep learning. Fails S3 criterion 1 (DL primary method) and criterion 5 (quantitative segmentation metrics). Fails v2 framework F-criteria as well: no versioned release/components/benchmark reproduction; it is a clinical platform paper, not a segmentation framework evaluation. Excluded papers are not routed to a study type.

exclusion_reason: Tutorial/introduction article (special issue: 'Introduction to Deep Learning in Medical Image Processing') that demonstrates an existing 3D U-Net architecture with a V-Net-style Dice loss on abdominal CT; presents no new method, architecture, or significant improvement — fails include criterion 6 (novel contribution) and triggers exclusion criterion 7 (applies existing methods without methodological contribution).
screening_notes: Meets most criteria superficially: 3D U-Net-like FCN (3x3x3 kernels, 64x64x64 subvolumes), 377 contrast-enhanced portal-venous abdominal CTs, multi-organ segmentation (liver, spleen, stomach, gallbladder, pancreas, artery, portal vein), quantitative Dice (89.3% +/- 6.5 test average). However, the article's stated purpose is pedagogical ('we describe how to build a 3D FCN'); the architecture is replicated from Cicek et al. 3D U-Net [21] and the loss from Milletari et al. V-Net [22] with uniform class weights; authors concede results are 'comparable' to prior work and that direct comparison is difficult due to differing datasets. The underlying novel contribution (hierarchical 3D FCN, arXiv:1704.06382, ref [44]) is published separately and should be screened instead. Confidence not higher because the demo experiment has real evaluation and could be argued as an application paper.

exclusion_reason: Exclusion criterion 7: applies an existing segmentation method without methodological contribution — the modified 3D U-Net with CycleGAN domain-transfer augmentation was developed in a separate technical publication (Sandfort et al., ref 24, 'submitted'); this paper only applies it. Also fails inclusion criterion 6: no segmentation metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff) reported — all quantitative evaluation (r²=0.93, ±2.7 HU agreement, steatosis-category sensitivity/specificity) measures downstream fat quantification, not segmentation accuracy.
screening_notes: Passes criteria 1-4 (3D U-Net as segmentation method, volumetric 256×256×192 processing, liver segmentation, nonenhanced CT). Fails on evaluation and novelty: segmentation performance is only reported indirectly as a 0.06% failure rate (7/11,676 scans); the paper's contribution is epidemiological (steatosis prevalence in n=9,552 cohort, longitudinal analysis), not a segmentation method or its evaluation. Primary purpose is liver fat quantification, using segmentation as a means.

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (Exclusion #7): the segmentation backbone (DpnUNet) is adopted from prior work (Wu et al.) and commercialized as RT-Mind-AI; the study's contribution is standard localized fine-tuning (Adam, class-weighted cross-entropy, 5-fold CV) plus clinical validation of a commercial product, not a new method, architecture, or methodological advance.
screening_notes: Borderline case. Meets: DL as primary method (DpnUNet), planning CT modality, quantitative metrics (DSC, 95HD, sensitivity, specificity), multi-structure segmentation. Fails Novel Contribution: no new architecture or training method is proposed; the claimed novelty (first fine-tuning study for rectal cancer DLAS, generalizability across CT simulators) is clinical/deployment-level, and the performance gains come from routine fine-tuning of an existing vendor model. Also targets CTV (non-organ) in addition to only 3 OARs (bladder, femoral heads, small intestine), and 3D convolutions are never explicitly stated (likely volumetric but unconfirmed). Would flip to INCLUDE only if the review scope counts commercial-model adaptation studies as methodological contributions.

exclusion_reason: Dosimetry pipeline paper (SimpleDose), not a CT organ segmentation paper. Fails multiple S3 criteria: (1) deep learning is not the primary method — the paper's contribution is a collapsed-cone-superposition dosimetry workflow; segmentation is a supporting step using off-the-shelf nnU-Net V2 trained on public datasets (TotalSegmentator, HaN-Seg), with no segmentation methodological contribution beyond an HU-threshold rule for bone marrow (exclusion criteria 2 and 7); (2) primary modality is whole-body SPECT/CT nuclear medicine dosimetry, not CT-based segmentation (exclusion criterion 4); (3) no segmentation metrics reported — no Dice, IoU, or Hausdorff anywhere; all quantitative results are dose-rate percentage deviations vs MIRDcalc/LDM (exclusion criterion 6 for segmentation evaluation, inclusion criterion 5 unmet).
screening_notes: nnU-Net V2 segments 23 whole-body structures on the CT component of SPECT/CT, so it superficially touches the review topic, but segmentation performance is never evaluated and the novelty claims (CCS dose kernel, automated multi/single-time-point dosimetry, SaaS deployment) all belong to radiopharmaceutical dosimetry. Also, evaluation is on 10 patients with dose-rate comparisons — no segmentation ground-truth comparison. Correct venue to route this is a dosimetry/theranostics review, not a 3D organ segmentation review. Not a framework paper per v2 routing (SimpleDose is a closed dosimetry SaaS, not an open-source segmentation toolkit; no license or versioned release reported).

exclusion_reason: Exclusion criterion 7: applies existing DL segmentation methods without methodological contribution. The modified 3D U-Net hepatosplenic segmentation tool was previously published (refs 15, 19, 20 in the paper: 'The methodology for automated hepatosplenic assessment has been previously described in detail'); this paper only applies that existing tool to a new clinical task (steatosis categorization on contrast-enhanced CT). Secondary support: no segmentation quality metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff) are reported — all quantitative results (ROC-AUC, sensitivity/specificity) evaluate HU attenuation thresholds for steatosis classification, not segmentation performance.
screening_notes: DL (modified 3D U-Net) is used and is volumetric on CT, and liver/spleen are segmented — but segmentation is instrumental infrastructure from prior work, not the paper's contribution. The novel element is clinical: HU threshold tables for PDFF-based steatosis categories. Fails INCLUDE criteria 5 (no segmentation metrics) and 6 (no segmentation methodological novelty). A clinical validation/application paper, out of scope for a review on 3D organ segmentation methods.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (exclusion criterion 3)
screening_notes: Paper uses a 2D U-Net applied slice-by-slice: authors explicitly state 'Due to the complexity of Networks such as 3DSegNet or the U-Net modifications, we decided to implement the 2D-U-Net', input is 512x512 slice images, downsampling is 2D (512x512 to 16x16), and the Limitations section confirms 'A 3D semantic segmentation architecture is still not possible with the DeepLTK'. The 'per volume' IoU is just slice-level aggregation, not volumetric processing. All other criteria pass (DL primary method: yes; lung organ: yes; CT: yes; IoU/Bland-Altman metrics: yes; minor contribution via LabVIEW/DeepLTK implementation with 32-filter modification), but the 2D-only processing fails the hard exclusion.

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution: the paper evaluates the commercial, pre-trained ART-Plan software (TheraPanacea, 3D U-Net based, Class IIb medical device) explicitly stating 'no fine-tuning was performed using institutional data'. The primary contribution is a clinical radiotherapy peer-review workflow assessment (comparing manual vs. AI vs. AI-adjusted contouring), not a new segmentation method, architecture, or algorithmic improvement.
screening_notes: Criteria check: (1) DL used but only as an off-the-shelf commercial tool; the study's focus is clinical workflow/peer review, not DL methodology. (2) 3D U-Net on volumetric CT sims - met. (3) Segments OARs (bladder, anorectum) and CTV (prostate + seminal vesicles); CTV is a clinical target volume rather than a purely anatomical organ, though OARs partially satisfy this. (4) CT modality - met. (5) Reports DSC and HDmax - met. (6) Novel contribution - NOT met: no new method, architecture, training, or significant segmentation improvement; authors describe it as 'a testing methodology to assess the impact of integrating AI-based auto-contouring software into the radiotherapy contouring workflow'. Additional concerns: AI contours (C_AI) are used as the reference/'ground truth', cohorts are temporally non-comparable (42 vs. 20 patients), and no GPU/training details exist since the model is external. Triggers EXCLUDE criterion 7 ('only applies existing methods without methodological contribution'). Not a framework paper: ART-Plan is commercial closed-source software, failing F1 (open-source requirement). Borderline aspects (real quantitative DSC/HDmax on CT with a 3D U-Net) keep confidence below 0.9.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context (EX-3). Secondary: applies existing ResU-Net architecture with standard preprocessing, no methodological contribution (EX-7).
screening_notes: DL is primary method, CT modality, liver organ segmentation, quantitative metrics (DSC, VOE, RVD) all present — but the 3D criterion fails hard. Volume is split into 2D slices; HU windowing, histogram equalization, and flip/90°-rotation augmentation are all per-slice; architecture is a standard 2D U-Net with 3x3 convs and residual blocks. No 3D convolutions, no volumetric aggregation, no inter-slice context anywhere in the paper. That is exactly the '2D slices independently' exclusion. Novelty is also thin: ResU-Net (residual U-Net) is pre-existing; contribution is 'implementation' plus off-the-shelf preprocessing (their own wording) on 3D-IRCADb (only 20 tumor-bearing scans used). Either exclusion alone is sufficient; EX-3 is the decisive one. Note: quoted abstract DSC values (0.97%, 0.83%) are unit errors; tables report 0.9781 liver / 0.893 tumor — irrelevant since excluded.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context. The paper explicitly adopts a 'classical 2D FCN model based on VGG-16 and 2D U-Net' and performs slice-by-slice training/classification with no 3D convolutions or inter-slice/volumetric context mechanism.
screening_notes: Meets most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (2D FCN, 2D U-Net in TensorFlow); CT modality; segments organs (liver, kidney, spleen); reports quantitative Dice (best liver 0.9789 mean with FCN); presents a novel contribution (pre-training-based hard/easy sample balancing for data augmentation). Fails inclusion criterion 2 / triggers exclusion rule 3: the networks operate on individual 2D slices independently; although data come from 3D CT volumes and results are visualized in 3D, there is no 3D context or volumetric processing in the method itself. Borderline because the data balancing operates at volume level, hence confidence 0.9 not 1.0.

exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric): the paper explicitly uses 2D networks processing CT slices independently, corresponding to exclusion criterion 3 (only 2D slices without 3D context). The authors state: 'each slice is one training sample in a 2D network' and 'Based on these above reasons, we decided to use 2D networks in our experiments' — they tested the 2.5D H-DenseUNet but rejected it due to GPU memory limits (batch size 1), with no 3D convolutions or inter-slice/volumetric context anywhere in the architecture.
screening_notes: Paper meets all other criteria: (1) deep learning (U-Net-derived CNN with Squeeze-and-Excitation connections, pyramid structure, auto-context cascade) is the primary method; (2) segments multiple anatomical organs (13 head-and-neck OARs: eyes, temporal lobes, mandibles, brainstem, parotids, submandibular glands, spinal cord, thyroid; plus liver on LiTS); (3) CT modality (private NPC head-and-neck CT dataset, 356 patients; LiTS public CT); (4) quantitative evaluation (Dice, Dice per case/global, precision, recall, 5-fold cross-validation; best mean Dice 83.28% on NPC OARs, liver Dice 85.47% per case on LiTS); (5) novel contribution (SEC skip-connection module, pyramid fusion, cascaded auto-context). However, the method is strictly 2D slice-wise — images resized to 256×256 and processed slice-by-slice — which fails the review's core 3D/volumetric requirement. Note: paper is otherwise a borderline-relevant 'method' study that reviewers of the full corpus may wish to flag as 2D-only OAR segmentation in CT.

exclusion_reason: Fails S3 criterion 3: processes 2D slices independently without 3D context. SED-1 (U-Net) and SED-2 (FC-DenseNet) take single-channel 256x256x1 2D slice inputs with 2D convolutions/pooling (Tables 1-2); the '3D' in the title is only post-hoc tumor contour reconstruction performed in Photoshop CC 2018 for visualization, not volumetric or 3D-convolutional processing. Secondary concern: the primary target is liver lesion/tumor segmentation; liver segmentation (SED-1) serves as a ROI pre-processing stage for tumor extraction (borderline vs. S3-EXCL-5).
screening_notes: Meets criteria 1 (CNN primary), 4 (CT), 5 (Dice/IoU/AUC reported), and arguably 6 (two-stage successive encoder-decoder). Fails criterion 2 decisively: architecture tables show 2D feature maps throughout (encoder input 256^2 x 1, per-slice processing, no 3D convolutions, no volumetric context). Explicit statement: 'Photoshop CC 2018 was used to achieve the 3D volume reconstruction of liver tumor' from adjacent 2D segmentation maps. Liver Dice 0.92, tumor Dice 0.75 on LiTS+KCGMH (4300 images).

exclusion_reason: Retracted paper — retraction notice published 26 August 2026 (Diagnostics 2026, 16, 2728). Retracted publications are ineligible for systematic review inclusion. Secondary concern: despite '3D-semantic segmentation' branding, the pipeline operates on 2D slices (GAN input 64x64x3, segmentation input 512x512x3; no 3D convolutions described), so criterion 2 (volumetric 3D processing) is not credibly met.
screening_notes: Retraction is explicit in title, watermark, and publisher note ('This paper has been retracted'). Even setting retraction aside: deep learning is primary (GAN + YOLOv3-ResNet-50 + DeepLabv3/InceptionResNetV2), CT modality (3D-IRCADb), liver organ + liver tumor segmented, and quantitative metrics reported (IoU 0.99, F1 0.995, accuracy) — but no Dice is reported, '3D' processing is slice-based, and much of the evaluation centers on tumor localization/segmentation. Retraction is decisive; no extraction performed.

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution. The paper is a clinical validation study of an existing, previously published deep learning model (Siemens AI-Rad Companion Research; architecture described in Jacob et al. 2023, ref [9]). The authors explicitly state the objective was to 'assess the accuracy of an existing deep learning model' and that 'algorithm development was done independently from and finalized prior to the results presented in this manuscript.' No new method, architecture, or improvement is presented.
screening_notes: Passes criteria 1-5 nominally: deep learning segmentation (image-to-image network + conditional VAE per ref [9]), 3D CT volumes, cardiac chamber/myocardium segmentation, non-contrast chest CT, quantitative evaluation (ICC, Bland-Altman — though no overlap metrics like Dice/Hausdorff are reported, only volume agreement). Fails criterion 6/EXCLUDE-7: no methodological contribution; model predates the study and was developed by Siemens Healthineers. This is a clinical application/validation paper, not a methods paper. Not a framework paper (closed, research-only commercial tool, no versioned release or benchmark reproduction).

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (exclusion criterion 7): the paper benchmarks off-the-shelf tools (RVX Semi-Automatic, RVX Deep Learning, TotalSegmentator in 3D Slicer) against manual segmentation. No new architecture, training, or method is developed; deep learning is an evaluated tool, not the paper's primary method (criterion 2).
screening_notes: Clinical validation/comparison study (86 contrast-enhanced abdominal CTs, single center). Meets CT (criterion 4), organ (liver, criterion 3), and metric (Dice 0.911-0.946, HD, Bland-Altman, criterion 5) requirements, but fails novelty (criterion 6): both DL tools are cited prior work (ref [15] R-Vessel-X, ref [16] TotalSegmentator) run as-is. No model is trained, modified, or improved. Also arguably fails criterion 1 (DL as primary method) since the paper is an agreement/efficiency study across manual, semi-automatic, and automatic approaches. Not a framework paper itself; it is a user of TotalSegmentator/RVX.

exclusion_reason: Fails Include Criterion 2 / triggers Exclude Criterion 3: the model processes 2D slices independently with no 3D context (input defined as X ∈ R^{H×W×C}, 2D 3×3 convolutions, pixel-accuracy metrics, 2D Euclidean distance transform, CT images resized to 150×150 px 2D colorized images, batching of 'MRI slices' and 'CT images'). Additionally triggers Exclude Criterion 4: the core segmentation and eGFR prediction task is trained and evaluated exclusively on T2-weighted MRI; the colorized CT dataset (12,446 label-free 2D images) is used only for external cross-modality robustness checks with no CT segmentation ground truth.
screening_notes: Novel dual-headed multitask U-Net (FG-CKD-UNet) for kidney compartment segmentation (cortex/medulla/pelvis) plus eGFR prediction with a structure-function consistency loss. DL is the primary method, the kidney is an organ, quantitative metrics are reported (Dice 0.94, HD95 9.8 mm), and the contribution is novel — so it passes criteria 1, 3, 5, 6. However, it fails the 3D/volumetric requirement: the architecture, equations, and preprocessing all operate on 2D slices (H×W×C inputs, 3×3 kernels, pixel-wise metrics, volumetric biomarkers computed by summing over 2D indices i,j). The 'kidney volume' biomarker is therefore not true volumetric analysis of a 3D CT volume. Regarding CT modality: the only CT data is a colorized 2D kidney image classification dataset (Normal/Cyst/Tumor/Stone) with no segmentation masks, used solely as an external evaluation set; the authors explicitly state that all segmentation learning, biomarker extraction, and eGFR prediction were trained and evaluated only on the T2-weighted MRI dataset. For a review on 3D organ segmentation from CT, this paper's primary modality is MRI and its processing is 2D, so it is excluded.

exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric) and triggers exclusion criterion 3: the paper explicitly adopts a 2D slice-based formulation — input is a single axial slice (256×256×1), all baselines were 'trained using 2D axial slices', and the authors state 3D context was intentionally avoided to reduce communication overhead. No 3D convolutions, 2.5D multi-view inputs, or inter-slice context are used; volumetric resampling (1mm³) is only preprocessing.
screening_notes: Otherwise strong candidate: novel deep learning architecture (FF-ResUNet, a skip-free collaborative residual U-Net) as primary method; segments liver (organ) + tumors on CT (LiTS, 3D-IRCADb, AMOS-CT); reports quantitative metrics (Dice 0.952 liver / 0.737 tumor, HD95, communication payload); clear methodological contribution (privacy-preserving split-learning design, multi-scale dilated decoder, boundary-aware loss, ablations). It satisfies criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 but unambiguously fails the 3D/volumetric requirement, so it is excluded despite its quality. Also note it is not a framework/tooling paper (no open-source platform release), so study-type routing would have been 'method' if included.

exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criteria 2 (3D/Volumetric) and 3 (Organ Segmentation). (a) The method operates on individual 2D axial slices only: '3D CT scans are preprocessed into 256 × 256 2D axial slices' with 'only axial slices containing the tumor... extracted', and the authors explicitly acknowledge 'the current framework's reliance on 2D slice processing... at the expense of ignoring critical volumetric context', deferring a 2.5D extension to future work (exclusion criterion 3: only processes 2D slices without 3D context; is_3d = false). (b) The paper segments lung TUMORS/lesions, not anatomical organs — 'automatic lung tumor segmentation' (exclusion criterion 5: only segments tumors/lesions, not organs).
screening_notes: The paper otherwise meets most criteria: deep learning is the primary method (hybrid ViT encoder + ASPP + attention-gated U-Net-like decoder, 136M params; LAURA variants down to ~5M), input is CT (MSD Task 06 Lung, NSCLC-Radiogenomics; 307 cases), quantitative metrics are extensively reported (Dice, Sensitivity, Specificity, GFLOPs, VRAM, inference time, statistical tests), and there is a clear novel contribution (new hybrid architecture plus federated learning framework with FedProx, adaptive weighted aggregation, dynamic virtual clients; best centralized Dice 84.24% on MSD Lung). However, exclusion is unambiguous: the title itself states '2D Hybrid Transformer', all convolutions are Conv2d with 256x256 single-slice inputs, the authors contrast their approach with 3D architectures like nnU-Net/UNETR, and the segmentation target is lung tumor rather than an anatomical organ. The federated-learning 'framework' framing does not qualify it as a tooling/platform paper (not MONAI/nnInteractive-style).

exclusion_reason: Fails inclusion criterion 2 (3D/Volumetric) and meets exclusion criterion 3 (only processes 2D slices without 3D context). The method is a purely 2D U-Net variant (2D convolutions with 3x3/1x1 kernels, ImageNet-pretrained 2D backbones ResNet34/SEResNext50) applied independently to slices extracted from CT volumes. The authors explicitly state the method 'is based on the processing of slice images from the original three-dimensional (3D) image so that our method does not require large computational resources' and that they 'used 2D images for training to save a massive amount of computing resources compared to 3D volumes'. No 3D convolutions or inter-slice volumetric context are used in the segmentation model; STAPLE is ensemble label-fusion post-processing across k-fold checkpoints, not volumetric segmentation context.
screening_notes: Borderline case that meets all other criteria: deep learning is the primary method (attention U-Net with GN); CT modality (SegTHOR, StructSeg 2019); organ segmentation (esophagus as OAR, though multi-class models output all thoracic OARs); quantitative metrics reported (Dice, HD/HD95); clear novel contribution (spatial attention decoder, group normalization, STAPLE-based k-fold fusion) with state-of-the-art claims (Dice 0.8690 on SegTHOR test via leaderboard; 0.7784 on StructSeg training set, outperforming SCSE/CBAM variants and MTL-WMCE). The sole disqualifying factor is the 2D/3D criterion: the network processes each slice independently with zero 3D operations. The volumetric elements present (slice extraction from 3D volumes, 3D reconstruction of outputs, STAPLE fusion on reconstructed volumes, 3D Dice/HD evaluation via challenge leaderboard, 3D visualization in Fig. 4) were considered but judged insufficient to constitute '3D context' in segmentation decisions, as no inter-slice information informs the model's predictions. Reviewers seeking to include 2D/2.5D slice-based pipelines evaluated on 3D volumes could reasonably include this paper, hence moderate confidence.

exclusion_reason: Only applies existing methods without methodological contribution (exclusion #7): the paper applies off-the-shelf V-Net (Milletari et al., 2016) unchanged — no architectural modification, new loss, or novel component; the pipeline (cropping, normalization, rotation/flipping augmentation) is standard. The claimed superiority (80% DSC vs. 58–72%) is unsupported because Table 1 compares against methods evaluated on entirely different datasets (ISBI cell tracking, ILD, NSCLC-Radiomics), not on Task06_Lung.
screening_notes: Meets DL (V-Net FCN), 3D (volumetric V-Net), CT (Task06_Lung/TCIA), organ (lung parenchyma, 98% DSC, in addition to tumor), and quantitative evaluation (DSC) criteria. Borderline on novelty: no modification to V-Net, no ablations, no same-dataset baselines; single small dataset (96 scans, 64 train/32 test) split from MSD Task06_Lung. If the review tolerates application-level studies, this would be INCLUDE as study_type 'method' — flagged as borderline rather than clear-cut.

exclusion_reason: Deep learning is not the primary segmentation method (Exclusion Criterion 2). The paper's core contribution is a deformable image registration pipeline (elastix, B-spline, multi-stage) for contour propagation in adaptive proton therapy; organ contours (prostate, seminal vesicles, lymph nodes, rectum, bladder) are produced by registration propagation, not by a deep network.
screening_notes: Borderline case. Satisfies 3D (3D convolutions), CT modality, quantitative metrics (DSC, MSD, 95% HD), and novelty criteria. However, DL plays only an auxiliary role: a 3D U-Net (essentially Çiçek et al. with minor modifications, e.g., strided convolutions) segments only the bladder to steer the registration cost function, and a 2D GAN inpaints rectal gas pockets. Reported DSC/MSD/HD results for prostate, SV, LN, rectum measure registration quality, not DL segmentation performance. Given the review focus on 3D organ segmentation using deep learning as the primary method, this is excluded despite the DL component.

exclusion_reason: Only processes 2D slices without 3D context
screening_notes: Passes DL focus (U-Net + residual modules, PyTorch), CT modality, quantitative metrics (Dice 0.87, IoU 0.77, Hausdorff 4.36mm), and segments an anatomical structure (left atrium). Fails 3D criterion decisively: paper states the model 'accepts two-dimensional axial CT image sections as input' and the volume segmentation is produced by feeding 'each axial section of the volume sequentially into the model' then concatenating 2D maps along z — slice-independent processing with no 3D context. Secondary concern: the methodological contribution is minimal (standard U-Net with residual modules and instance normalization; no hyperparameter search), as the paper's primary novelty is the clinical finding (LA volume as AF biomarker), which also weakly triggers the 'applies existing methods without methodological contribution' criterion.
